subject: English
topic: Articles and Prepositions — Correct Usage in Context (W11 B1)

questions.stem:
Fill in the blank with the correct article:
'He is ___ honest man who never tells lies.'
questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Honest' begins with a silent 'h' — the first sound is the vowel /ɒ/. Therefore use 'an' (the rule is based on SOUND, not spelling). Other words with silent h: hour, heir, honour. Compare: 'a hotel' (h is pronounced /h/, so 'a'), but 'an honest man' (h is silent). Trap: 'a' is wrong because 'a' precedes consonant sounds; 'the' would make him a specific man already mentioned (not the case here).

questions.stem:
Choose the correct article:
'She plays ___ violin in the city orchestra.'
questions.explanation: C is correct. 'The' is used before musical instruments when playing them (standard British English rule). 'She plays the violin / the piano / the guitar.' Trap: 'a violin' implies she plays a non-specific violin (object-focused, not the conventional music-playing idiom); 'an' is phonetically wrong before 'violin' (v = consonant sound).

questions.stem:
Choose the correct preposition:
'She has been working ___ this company ___ 2018.'
questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Work in a company' (not 'for' when referring to being employed within an organisation). 'Since 2018' = from a specific point in time up to now (used with perfect tenses). Trap: 'for' = duration (for 5 years), not a year-point; 'with' = alongside/together (not the standard preposition for employment in an organisation); 'from' = starting point (used with 'to' not 'have been').

questions.stem:
Choose the correct article:
'I have a dog and a cat. ___ dog is brown.'
questions.explanation: C is correct. 'The' is used for a specific noun already introduced in the conversation. 'I have a dog' (first mention = 'a'). '___ dog is brown' (second mention, now specific = 'the'). This is the golden rule of 'a/an' for first mention and 'the' for subsequent mentions. Trap: 'A dog' = reintroduces the dog as if it's a new dog (wrong); 'No article' = wrong because a specific dog is being referred to.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct preposition:
'The teacher was very angry ___ the students who failed to submit their assignments.'
questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Angry WITH a person' is the correct collocation when the anger is directed at a person. Trap: 'Angry AT' = used for a thing or situation (angry at the delay/mistake), not a person; 'angry about' = indirect anger about an issue, not directly at the person; 'angry on' is simply incorrect in standard English.

questions.stem:
Fill in the blank:
'He is ___ MBA from IIM Ahmedabad.'
questions.explanation: B is correct. 'MBA' is pronounced letter-by-letter as /em-bee-ey/. The first sound is /em/ = a vowel sound. So use 'an'. Rule: use 'an' before ACRONYMS that begin with a vowel sound when read aloud (MBA, MLA, FIR, SSC, IPS). Use 'a' for consonant-sound acronyms (BA, MA pronounced as words). 'An MBA' / 'An MLA' / 'An FIR' / 'A BJP leader'. Trap: 'a MBA' ignores the pronunciation rule.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct preposition:
'The flight departs ___ Delhi and arrives ___ London.'
questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Depart FROM a city' (starting point). 'Arrive IN a city' (large location — city, country, continent). Compare: 'arrive AT a specific place/small location' (arrive at the airport, at the hotel). 'Arrive IN London' = correct for a city. 'Arrive AT London Heathrow' would be correct for the specific airport. Trap: 'arrive at London' treats London as a specific point — acceptable in informal speech but 'in' is standard for cities.

questions.stem:
Identify the correct sentence:
(A) She is the best student of the class.
(B) She is best student of the class.
(C) She is a best student of the class.
(D) She is best student in class.
questions.explanation: A is correct. 'The best' = superlative requires 'the' (definite article before superlatives). 'The best student of the class' is fully correct. Trap: B misses 'the' before 'best' (mandatory before superlatives); C uses 'a' with a superlative — impossible, as 'the best' implies uniqueness (only one 'best'); D omits 'the' before both 'best' and 'class'.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct preposition:
'He has been suffering ___ fever ___ the last three days.'
questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Suffer FROM a disease/ailment' (fever, cold, pain) is the standard idiom. 'FOR the last three days' = duration (three-day period). Trap: 'suffer with' = informal (sometimes used but 'from' is standard for SSC); 'since the last three days' = wrong ('since' requires a specific point, not a period — 'since Monday', not 'since three days').

questions.stem:
Choose the correctly formed sentence:
(A) He is interested to learn piano.
(B) He is interested in learning the piano.
(C) He is interested for learning piano.
(D) He is interested about learning the piano.
questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Interested IN + gerund (verb-ing)' is the fixed preposition collocation. 'He is interested in learning' — not 'to learn' (interested takes IN, not infinitive without 'in'). 'The piano' uses 'the' before musical instruments (as established). Trap: A — 'interested to learn' uses infinitive without preposition (non-standard); C — 'for learning' is wrong (interested takes 'in'); D — 'about' changes the meaning subtly (interested about = curious about a topic, but 'interested in learning' = wants to learn).
